title: Nasdaq Nears Record High as Dow, S&P Climb Post‑Jobs Report; Treasury Yields Pull Back
body:
The U.S. equity market closed Friday on a broadly upbeat note, with the Nasdaq Composite nudging within striking distance of an all‑time high, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 each posted modest gains. The rally was sparked by a softer‑than‑expected jobs report for September, which eased concerns about a tightening labor market and its impact on corporate earnings. Bond investors initially welcomed the data, pushing Treasury yields lower, but the respite was short‑lived as yields quickly reversed course and finished the session higher.

The Nasdaq’s climb of roughly 0.6 % left the index just a few points shy of its record peak set earlier this year, underscoring the resilience of technology‑heavy stocks despite lingering macroeconomic headwinds. The Dow added 0.4 % and the S&P 500 rose 0.5 %, driven largely by gains in consumer discretionary, industrials and health‑care sectors. Market participants pointed to the September jobs numbers, which showed a slower pace of hiring and a marginal dip in the unemployment rate, as a sign that the Federal Reserve’s aggressive rate‑hiking cycle may be losing steam. The data suggested that employers are still cautious, giving the Fed room to pause or even consider a modest easing in the coming months.

Analysts cautioned, however, that the optimism may be tempered by the bond market’s reaction. Treasury yields on the 10‑year note fell to 4.27 % after the jobs report, only to rebound to 4.31 % by the close. The brief dip reflected a typical “flight to safety” response, but the subsequent climb indicated that investors remain wary of inflationary pressures and the prospect of higher rates persisting longer than anticipated. The yield curve’s flattening – with the two‑year note edging higher as well – suggests that short‑term rate expectations are still anchored to a more hawkish stance, even as longer‑term yields respond to the softer labor data.

The mixed signals from equities and bonds highlight a market in transition. On one hand, the equity rally shows that investors are betting on corporate profitability and a potential slowdown in rate hikes. On the other hand, the bond market’s quick reversal points to lingering uncertainty about the Fed’s next move and the durability of the current inflation trajectory. “We’re seeing a classic tug‑of‑war between growth optimism and monetary tightening,” said a senior market strategist at a major brokerage. “The jobs report gave a temporary boost, but the underlying macro backdrop remains fragile.”

Looking ahead, market watchers will focus on the upcoming Federal Open Market Committee meeting, scheduled for next week, where policymakers are expected to signal whether the current rate trajectory will continue or shift toward a more accommodative stance. In addition, the release of October’s employment figures and the Consumer Price Index will provide further clues on the economy’s momentum. If the labor market continues to soften and inflation shows signs of easing, equities could sustain their upward drift, potentially pushing the Nasdaq over the record line. Conversely, any surprise uptick in inflation or a more aggressive Fed stance could reignite bond‑market pressure, pulling yields higher and weighing on risk‑assets.

For now, the market’s ability to absorb mixed data and maintain forward momentum suggests that investors are cautiously optimistic. The interplay between employment trends, monetary policy, and investor sentiment will shape the next leg of the rally, with the Nasdaq poised either to break its record or retreat, depending on how the economic narrative unfolds in the weeks ahead.
